extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and voters of New York; delegates and the general public engaged in the Constitutional ratification debate
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the normative standards and practical principles Hamilton (Publius) advances for structuring federal power — especially regarding use of force, militia regulation, and the federal power of taxation — intended to guide constitutional design and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of force in emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government may be necessitated to resort to force in certain emergencies (seditions, insurrections) — governing solely by regular law is unrealistic in such cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergencies of this sort sometimes arise in all societies; when they do, there is no remedy but force. The means must be proportioned to the extent of the mischief (e.g., militia for a slight commotion; different force if insurrection pervades a whole State). This principle rebuts the objection that the possibility of national force argues against the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must be proportioned to ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods used to preserve order must be appropriate to the scale of the threat: small disturbances can be suppressed by local militia; extensive insurrections may require a differently constituted force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: militia adequate for a slight commotion in a small part of a State; if insurrection pervades a whole State, the State itself has raised regular troops. The rule ‘means proportioned to the end’ is applied to justify varied response levels and to counter fears of a uniform military instrument for all contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection equally applies to States and Union (consistency of objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument that a national government might need a force other than the militia applies tenfold to plans that create multiple small confederacies or to individual States themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton points out that Massachusetts and Pennsylvania had recourse to raising troops; if a State (e.g., New York) attempted large enterprises (re-establishing jurisdiction), it would need regular forces. Therefore the possibility of the Union requiring such force is not a unique objection to a general government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government as primary security
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrating power in representatives of the people is the essential and most efficacious security for rights and privileges attainable in civil society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the proposed government vests power in people's representatives, that representative character is regarded as the main safeguard against abuse; its full efficacy is to be examined further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of self-defense against usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: If representatives betray their constituents, the original right of self-defense remains paramount and may be more effective against national usurpations than state usurpations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a single State, citizens lack distinct subordinate governments and must resort to disorganized resistance; in a federal system, citizens can use other States or the national structure to oppose usurpation in a more organized fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of territory increases resistance and decreases usurpation risk
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater territorial extent makes successful usurpation more difficult and facilitates popular resistance, provided citizens understand and defend their rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller territories allow usurpers to detect and crush opposition more readily; larger ones increase obstacles for usurpers and provide opportunities for other States to intervene or supply fresh forces, undermining attempts at centralized despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual checks among governments (federal/state balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power being rival to power, the general government and State governments will check each other; citizens can leverage one against the other to protect rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a confederacy the people may use the general government to check the States and vice versa; cherishing the union preserves this advantage and provides an instrument of redress if either level invades rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal regulation of the militia as incident to common defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to regulate the militia and command its services in times of insurrection and invasion is a natural incident to superintending the common defense and internal peace of the Confederacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity in organization and discipline yields beneficial effects (mutual intelligence and concert) when militias are called into service; federal direction is therefore proper to obtain this uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve to States of officers' appointment and training authority
rubrics_metrics.description: While Congress may ‘provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia,’ the Constitution reserves to the States the appointment of officers and the authority to train the militia according to discipline prescribed by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This division is presented as a compromise: national regulation secures uniformity and usefulness, while state appointment of officers and training preserves local control and mitigates fears of federal domination over the militia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia as a substitute for standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-regulated militia under competent control is the best substitute for standing armies and will lessen the call for permanent military establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the federal government can command militia aid in emergencies, it can better dispense with maintaining a different (standing) force. Effective militia organization reduces incentive for standing armies, which are argued to be dangerous to liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticality and undesirability of disciplining the whole populace
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to discipline the entire body of citizens to the level of a regular army is impracticable, burdensome to labor, and would not be endured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring the entire yeomanry to perform continual military exercises would impose major deductions from productive labor and public inconvenience; therefore, only modest aims (properly armed populace and occasional assembly) are reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a select corps of moderate extent
rubrics_metrics.description: A practicable plan is to form a select corps of moderate extent, well-trained and fit for service, rather than disciplining the whole nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumscribing the plan makes it possible to have an excellent body ready to take the field, which diminishes the need for a standing army and provides a counterbalance in case a regular army is formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authority to require citizen assistance (posse comitatus implied)
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government’s implied powers (necessary and proper to execute its powers) include requiring citizen aid (posse comitatus) to assist officers in executing the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omissions of an explicit posse comitatus provision do not imply absence of power; reasoning from necessary-and-proper authority shows that requiring citizens' assistance to enforce laws is inherent in executing declared powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interstate militia deployment for mutual succor
rubrics_metrics.description: It is natural and proper for the militia of a neighboring State to be marched into another to resist a common enemy or to guard the republic against violence of faction or sedition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual succor was practiced in the late war and is a principal end of political association; placing the power of affording it under Union direction prevents neglect of a neighbor’s danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: General power of taxation necessary for national functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government must have a general power of taxation to support national forces, pay the civil list, discharge national debts, and finance all other disbursements from the national treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money is the 'vital principle' of the body politic; without a complete power to procure adequate supplies the government risks continual plunder or fatal atrophy. The Constitution must interweave a general taxing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: National ability to raise revenues directly (not rely on requisitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting the national government to raise its own revenues by ordinary taxation (rather than depending on requisitions and quotas from States) is necessary to avoid the vices of the Confederation's finance system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requisitions proved unreliable in practice, weakening the Union and sowing discord. Direct taxing powers prevent dependence on intermediate State agencies and the resulting instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between internal and external taxation is unsound
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed separation (reserving internal taxation to States and external duties to the Union) violates the maxim that every power ought to be proportioned to its object; commercial imposts alone will not meet national exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting the federal resource to imposts would leave it in tutelage to the States and insufficient to meet debt, defense, and other national obligations; powers must match the breadth of national objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation powers preserve public credit and borrowing capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: A national power to create new funds by taxation enables the government to borrow effectively and maintain public credit; reliable taxation reassures lenders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without authority to create funds, the government would be driven to divert appropriated funds in emergencies, destroying credit. The power to tax supports borrowing so that loans can be secured in times of need.

rubrics_metrics.name: A government half supplied cannot fulfill its purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: A government that is under-supplied and constantly necessitous cannot provide security, advance prosperity, sustain reputation, or undertake enlarged public plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent deficiency leads to temporizing expedients, degraded administration, sacrifices of engagements, and inability to support large wartime expenditures or to command respect abroad; thus unconfined taxation authority is urged as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: powers must be commensurate with objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundational political axiom: every power ought to be commensurate with its object; where the purpose is unlimited, a corresponding limitation on the power is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton frames this as a primary truth underpinning the case for broad national powers: means must be adequate to ends and cannot be artificially truncated when the object admits no limitation.
